solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: One clearing up mess decks with basket

parts.note: poops are the raised decks at a ship's stern
a coop can be a wicker basket, as for hens or fish

explanation.surface: A sailor tidying the mess decks, basket in hand.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'mess decks' picture breaks apart: 'mess' belongs to the definition, 'decks' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A pooper-scooper is the tool dog owners use to pick up their animal's droppings, a literal mess.

clue.text: Devoutly hopes to hear appreciative remarks

indicators.note: to hear means the words for appreciative remarks are taken by their sound

parts.note: praise is appreciative comment

explanation.surface: A performer earnestly hoping for compliments.
explanation.definitionFit: To pray for something is to hope for it devoutly, as in a prayer.

clue.text: Playwright, one who asked for more money, a forger

parts.note: Oliver Twist famously asked for more gruel
gold is money or wealth
a smith is one who forges metal

explanation.surface: A dramatist who begged for more money and turned to forgery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'forger' suggests a fraudster but means a metalworker at a forge.
explanation.definitionFit: Oliver Goldsmith was the 18th-century Irish author of the comedy She Stoops to Conquer.

clue.text: Starry team? One that is

parts.note: a side is a team
something real is one that is, i.e. exists

explanation.surface: Asking whether a team is full of stars, and finding one that is.
explanation.definitionFit: Sidereal means relating to the stars, as in sidereal time measured against them.

clue.text: Disabled, needing oxygen by the sea

parts.note: O is the chemical symbol for oxygen
by means near, beside
the Med is the Mediterranean Sea

explanation.surface: A disabled person needing fresh seaside air.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone one-armed has lost the use of an arm, a physical disability.

clue.text: Pictures about one American pope

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the word for pictures goes around the rest

parts.note: pix is informal for pictures
I is the Roman numeral for one
US for American

explanation.surface: Photographs of a single American pope.
explanation.definitionFit: Pius IX was the 19th-century pope who called the First Vatican Council.

clue.text: Madly busy chap I see talking

parts.note: a chap is a man
taken as written

indicators.note: talking means the last word is taken by its spoken sound, not its spelling

parts.note: the letter C is pronounced like the word see

explanation.surface: A frantic man chattering about how busy he is.
explanation.definitionFit: Manic describes frenzied, hyperactive energy, which is being madly busy.

clue.text: Reason I'm confused with vote

indicators.note: confused means muddled, so the letters are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
taken as written

explanation.surface: A voter muddled about why they are voting.
explanation.definitionFit: A motive is the reason behind an action.

clue.text: Is Douglas linked with England? So Donne told us

parts.note: surface reading: a question about some connection between a man named Douglas and England
setter's reading: Douglas is the capital of the Isle of Man, and the reply is that this territory is cut off by sea, quoting Donne's sermon

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about Douglas and England, answered by a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Douglas is the capital of the Isle of Man in the Irish Sea; the answer reads as 'No: Man is an island', while also being John Donne's famous line.
explanation.definitionFit: John Donne wrote these words in his Meditation XVII, arguing every person is part of mankind.

clue.text: The up platform?

parts.note: surface reading: the railway platform for up trains, those heading to London
setter's reading: a lookout perch high up a ship's mast

explanation.surface: A passenger asking which station platform serves trains towards London.
explanation.walkthrough: In British railway usage the up line runs towards London, so the clue sounds like a station question.
explanation.definitionFit: A crow's nest is the lookout platform fixed near the top of a ship's mast, literally up high.

clue.text: Girl abandoned opera part, close to return

parts.note: an aria is a solo song in an opera

indicators.note: something made to return goes back the way it came, so the word for close is read backwards

parts.note: a close is an end

explanation.surface: A girl walks out on an opera role just before it comes back round.
explanation.walkthrough: Ariadne helped Theseus escape the Minotaur's labyrinth, and he then deserted her on Naxos.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Ariadne is the princess Theseus left behind on an island, the classic abandoned girl.

clue.text: Promoted, work was satisfying — returned lively!

parts.note: someone promoted has moved up

indicators.note: returned means going back, so the words for work and was satisfying are read backwards together

parts.note: OP is short for opus, a work
to meet a need is to satisfy it

explanation.surface: After a satisfying promotion, someone comes back in high spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: An up-tempo piece of music is played at a fast, lively pace.

clue.text: Guide always follows the way

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way
e'er is the poetic contraction of ever, meaning always

explanation.surface: A guide who is forever following the route.
explanation.walkthrough: 'follows' places the word for always after the word for the way.
explanation.definitionFit: To steer something is to guide its direction.

clue.text: Is not the first to discover discharge in kidneys

definitions.text: Is not the first to discover

indicators.note: in places the word for discharge inside the word for kidneys

parts.note: reins is an old word for the kidneys or loins
to vent is to let out or discharge

explanation.surface: A doctor who was beaten to a discovery about kidney discharges.
explanation.walkthrough: Reins for kidneys is archaic, surviving in the Bible and in 'renal'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who reinvents comes up with a thing already devised, so they were not the first to find it.

clue.text: On publication day, beer at New College

parts.note: a mag is a magazine, a publication
D is the abbreviation for day
ale is a kind of beer
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Drinking beer on publication day at New College, Oxford.
explanation.walkthrough: New College is itself an Oxford college, which makes 'New' look part of the definition; Magdalen is another Oxford college, pronounced 'maudlin'.
explanation.definitionFit: Magdalen is one of the colleges of Oxford University.

clue.text: Cocktail to pick up at lunchtime perhaps reluctantly at first, a small quantity

indicators.note: in a down clue, picking up lifts the letters so they read from bottom to top

parts.note: lunchtime might be one o'clock, so at lunchtime is at one, written AT I

indicators.note: at first keeps only the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: the opening letter of reluctantly
taken as written
a gram is a small unit of weight

explanation.surface: Someone reluctantly ordering just a small drink at lunchtime.
explanation.walkthrough: I is the Roman numeral for one, and one o'clock is a typical lunchtime.
explanation.definitionFit: A margarita is a cocktail of tequila, lime and orange liqueur.

clue.text: A female tennis ace

parts.note: taken as written
she is the female pronoun

explanation.surface: A woman who is a top tennis player.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a woman player, but Arthur Ashe was a man.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Ashe was a champion American player who won Wimbledon in 1975.

clue.text: Morale so bad in auction house

indicators.note: bad means in poor shape, so the letters are put into a different arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Spirits are low among the staff of an auction house.
explanation.definitionFit: A saleroom is the room or premises where auctions are held.

clue.text: Unusual form of capital Y

indicators.note: a form of something is a new shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A capital Y written in an odd style.
explanation.definitionFit: Atypical means not typical, so unusual.

clue.text: Actually withdrawing a pound in bank

indicators.note: withdrawing means taking out, so these letters are removed from the word for actually

parts.note: really means actually
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for a pound, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: Actually taking a pound out at the bank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bank' looks like the place for withdrawing money but is the verb, as in bank on.
explanation.definitionFit: To bank on someone is to rely on them; both mean to depend.

clue.text: Two aliens, one with no answer for hard taskmaster

indicators.note: with no means lacking, so one of the aliens loses a letter

parts.note: one alien: a Martian, from Mars
A is the abbreviation for answer
the other alien: ET, the extra-terrestrial of the film

explanation.surface: Two aliens, one of them unhelpfully silent, are put up for a strict boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two aliens' supplies both: Martian, then ET; the one with no answer is Martian without its A.
explanation.definitionFit: A martinet is a strict disciplinarian, named after a 17th-century French army drillmaster.

clue.text: Sweet little thing in city retreat

parts.note: EC is the postcode of the City of London
a lair is a den or hiding place to retreat to

explanation.surface: A sweet little person hiding away in the city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet little thing' sounds like a term of endearment for a person.
explanation.definitionFit: An eclair is a small cream-filled pastry, a little sweet treat.

clue.text: Express disappointment in feeble books

parts.note: a lame excuse is a feeble one
NT is the New Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: A reader let down by some weak books.
explanation.definitionFit: To lament is to voice grief or regret about something.

clue.text: Couple like party not to end? Time I'm going

indicators.note: not to end means the party is cut short, losing its last letter

parts.note: as means like
a social is a party

indicators.note: going means departing, so those two letters leave the word for time

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A guest at an endless party announcing it's time to leave.
explanation.definitionFit: To couple two things is to link or associate them.

clue.text: Assume one is in position

indicators.note: is in places the numeral for one inside the word for position

parts.note: a post is a position, as in a job; that the whole answer also starts the word position is a coincidence
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone presumes a person already holds the job.
explanation.definitionFit: To posit something is to put it forward as a premise, to assume it.

clue.text: Obsequious type turning up these days for radio programme

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up flips letters so they read upwards

parts.note: a toady is a fawning flatterer
AD, anno domini, marks the present era

explanation.surface: A sycophant appearing nowadays on a radio show.
explanation.walkthrough: The AD already sitting inside the flatterer's name is the part that turns. Today is BBC Radio 4's flagship morning news programme.
explanation.definitionFit: Today is the long-running BBC Radio 4 morning news and current affairs show.

clue.text: Limit a territory parrot is kept in

indicators.note: is kept in says the answer is held inside the run of words before it

parts.note: the letters run across limit, a and territory

explanation.surface: Restricting the patch of ground where a parrot is kept.
explanation.walkthrough: 'parrot' looks like the creature kept in a territory, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To parrot is to repeat or copy mindlessly, as parrots mimic speech.

clue.text: Old Lionheart spitting out one fruit here

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for old

indicators.note: spitting out means expelling, so the king's name loses that letter

parts.note: Richard I of England was called the Lionheart
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An old king spitting out a piece of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spitting out one fruit' reads as eating, but 'fruit here' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An orchard is a place where fruit trees grow, so fruit is found there.

clue.text: Hate Hobart, shivering when temperature drops

indicators.note: shivering means trembling, so the remaining letters are shaken into a new order
drops means falls away, so the abbreviation for temperature leaves the city's name

parts.note: taken as written: the capital of Tasmania
T is the abbreviation for temperature

explanation.surface: Someone loathes Hobart in winter, shivering as the temperature falls.
explanation.definitionFit: To abhor something is to detest or loathe it.

clue.text: Collapsed, going by railway? Don't use the line?

parts.note: to tumble is to fall down or collapse
RY is the abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: A train passenger told not to use the railway line.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is a washing line, not a railway line: tumble-dry clothes instead of hanging them out.
explanation.definitionFit: To tumble-dry laundry is to dry it in a machine rather than pegging it on a clothes line.
